components.text: The historical claim that Jesus's universal charity teaching caused a durable Western transformation.
Explain the historical origin and transmission of universal charity in the West.
The analogy from mind-independent historical and scientific facts to accessible mind-independent moral facts.
Show that mind-independent truth can amount to accessible moral knowledge for human reasoners.
The claim that subjective cognitive mediation deprives humans of direct access to objective moral truth.
Establish that subjective cognitive mediation prevents meaningful access to objective moral truth.
The proposed domain-specific route for obtaining objective moral knowledge despite subjective cognition.
The distinction between objective truth and beliefs, preferences, or attitudes concerning it.
Infer an objective moral standard from the felt or asserted rightness of moral judgments.
Provide a domain-specific route that positively establishes access to objective moral truth.
The claim that evolved human inclination can constitute morality without an objective standard.
Explain how inclination alone can justify superiority judgments and genuine moral progress.
The claim that genuine moral progress requires an objective standard beyond evolved human inclination.
Explain how inclination-based morality can warrant superiority and genuine moral progress.
Show that historical variation is compatible with mind-independent moral facts.
Show how domain-specific inquiry establishes objective moral knowledge.
The inference from historically late universal aid to morality's subjective or merely contingent status.
Jesus introduced a universal ethic that strongly influenced later Western moral concern.
Show whether late emergence of universal charity entails that morality itself is subjective.
Explain Jesus’s historical causal role in universal charity.
Supply an objective ground for the value of people aided.
The asserted historical absence of universal aid as evidence against enduring common morality.
Jesus's distinctive role in expanding concern beyond prior moral practice.
Reconcile late universal-aid practice with an enduring objective moral order.
Account for Jesus’s distinctive contribution to moral history.
Show that shared moral conscience is more than changing inclination.
The inference from cross-cultural common moral principles to objective morality or superior-being grounding.
Infer objective or divinely bestowed morality from cross-cultural moral commonality.
Defend divine-image dignity as an objective ground.
The objection that cross-cultural similarity does not deductively demonstrate objective or divinely bestowed morality.
Determine what common moral beliefs establish without treating them as a deductive proof of God.
Reconcile earlier commonality with Jesus’s later distinctive influence.
The historical claim that Jesus universalized aid beyond kin and social groups.
The claim that this teaching produced a worldwide or Western moral transformation.
Determine whether universalized outgroup care was merely historical change or genuine moral improvement.
Accept and assess the significance of the claimed worldwide transformation.
Explain whether inclinations can generate genuine obligations to aid.
The demand for grounds of moral belief and obligation beyond historically produced inclination.
The claim that inclination without objectivity cannot ground moral evaluation or action.
Explain what grounds moral belief and action if there is no external objective standard.
Explain how human inclinations justify claims of superiority or progress.
Compare human nature with objective truth as explanations of common beliefs.
The inference from deep, evolved, constitutive human inclinations to genuine normative grounds for moral action.
The proposal that felt inclination can constitute morality without an external standard.
Show that evolved inclinations possess normative authority rather than merely causal or motivational force.
Explain why one inclination is better or more binding than another.
The claim that guilt and perceived need for forgiveness are better explained by an objective moral code.
Provide a nonrealist explanation for guilt without presupposing an objective moral code.
The attempt to use guilt and moral argument to connect historical transformation with objective morality and God.
The broader challenge that an evolutionary account cannot supply objective normative authority.
Separate explanatory claims about historical transformation from claims about objective wrongdoing and divine grounding.
Explain the normative authority of evolved moral feelings.
Determine whether transformation was genuine objective improvement.
The claim that the historical transformation account can stand independently of moral objectivity or belief in God.
The evolutionary explanation offered for morality and guilt.
Identify what explanatory question remains after granting that the historical thesis is logically independent of metaethics.
Accept the occurrence of a major historical transformation.
Compare the evolutionary moral account with broader worldview explanations.
